newsitem.title: UK: Feverish European naphtha market seen cooling off.
newsitem.headline: Feverish European naphtha market seen cooling off.

text.p: The European naphtha market, normally the little kid on the block among the giant oil contracts, shot up this month as the rest of the complex turned sharply lower.

But traders and analysts warned that the rally was built like a house of cards, and that as soon as certain prompt demand requirements were met, prices could fall sharply from their post-Gulf War highs near $230 a tonne.
Seasonal factors, the lure of cheeper feedstocks and a correction in its spread versus crude and other products should all weigh on naphtha prices, they said.
When that exactly will happen has become a mystery shrouded by the maneouvres of a few traders.
"I think it can rapidly fall $40 to $190 (a tonne)," said a trader at one of the largest end-users in Europe.
"But I would say this whole situation isn't over yet because I still have the impression this game is going on," he said. "In my opinion (a price drop) should have happened a long time ago."

Naphtha with a so-called high paraffinic content is used as a feedstock for ethylene crackers. Naphtha with a high naphthenic and aromatic content, dubbed N+A, is preferred as a feedstock for reformers to make gasoline.

A few traders are believed to be short material of a certain size and quality that needs to be sent to an end-user this month, which has helped keep physical prices about $64 or 39 percent above their year-ago levels.
The higher bids were believed to be offset by profitable long positions in the swaps market.
The swaps trading positions could not be confirmed.
Some smaller cargoes are trading closer to $215-$220, one downside target pinpointed once the prompt demand lightens up.
The crack spread between naphtha prices, including cost, insurance and freight, and crude oil has blown out to 5-1/2 year highs between $60 and $70 a tonne.
Some traders expected that spread to narrow back to between $40 and $50 in coming weeks as the end-users balk at these higher levels and start to focus on March.
Gasoline prices are now trading below naphtha, a phenomenon normally seen in winter as petrol demand drops.

"I think inevitably we're expecting naphtha prices to weaken, especially relative to gasoline, in the next month or two, and generally weaken versus other products," said Colin Birch, a consultant at Purvin and Gertz in London.
He expected Northwest Europe cargoe prices to average $192 a tonne in 1997, down slightly from $195 last year.

Naphtha demand is running about 40 million tonnes per year, or 6.5 percent of total European products demand of 630 million tonnes, he said. Demand, while volatile from year to year, will likely grow two percent annually, he said.
A sharp drop in liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) may have mitigated the naphtha squeeze, sources said.

European propane prices plummeted $100 a tonne last week to $245/$250 cif last week and traders said it was speeding towards "cracking levels" -- the point at which the product could be used as a petchem feedstock.
"For the petrochemical companies, with LPG down and gas oil down, alternative feedstocks look more attractive to naphtha...We're seeing it happen now," a broker said.
"Naphtha is pricing itself out of the market," he said. "I think in principle it is right by saying the market is overvalued."
